signals.title: RL infrastructure at Microsoft AI | Microsoft AI
signals.excerpt:
Long, stable, and numerically accurate Reinforcement Learning (RL) is an essential piece of Microsoft AI’s (MAI) path to Humanist Superintelligence. We aim to climb capabilities from the base model through RL itself, which means runs of many thousands of training steps spanning weeks to months on thousands of GPUs, rather than a short RL phase at the end of post-training. Over runs that long, small numerical mismatches and system inefficiencies compound, so we built Rocket, MAI’s in-house RL framework, to enable us to post-train models at increasing scale. We recently shared an update on our new three-trillion-parameter base model, MAI Base 2, in Frontier Pre-training at Microsoft AI. MAI Base 2 is now being post-trained with Rocket, climbing from the base model through RL without distillation from third-party models. This work is separate from the MAI Code 2 models.

...

The MAI Thinking 1 technical report introduced Rocket as the RL framework which post-trained our previous pre-trained model, MAI Base 1, into the reasoning model MAI Thinking 1. Since then, we have improved Rocket to operate at the larger scale demanded by MAI Base 2. RL infrastructure needs to address many challenges at increasing scale:

1. Staleness. Agentic rollouts can take hours while the learner keeps updating the policy. Because GRPO scores each rollout against the others for the same problem, a single slow or failed rollout holds back its entire group, so training drifts further off-policy.
2. Numerical consistency. Fitting a larger model and longer contexts into the sampler requires lower-precision storage, and differences in precision, kernels, and parallelism between the sampler and learner can slow learning and destabilize training.
3. Fault tolerance and elasticity. Runs that span thousands of GPUs for weeks or months will encounter hardware failures, while the best runtime configuration and data mixture change. Restarting the whole job for every failure or reconfiguration wastes GPU time, so the system must recover and reconfigure components while the run continues.

...

MAI develops and operates three tightly connected systems necessary for RL: the learner and training framework, Rocket, and an inference engine built on an MAI-maintained fork of SGLang. Owning all three allows us to co-design the interfaces between them rather than optimize each component in isolation.

This does not mean building every layer from scratch. Rocket leverages Kubernetes or Slurm to allocate nodes to a job, and Rocket’s components run on Ray as actors. We adopted SGLang as our inference foundation and have substantially adapted it to MAI’s models and long-running agentic RL workloads. Owning these integrations carries a maintenance cost, but lets us evolve the complete RL loop rather than optimize its components in isolation. A future blog post will detail the ways that we adapted SGLang to fit our workloads.

signals.title:
From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval
            
            
            - Google Developers Blog
signals.excerpt:
NOV. 24, 2026

 Yingxin Jiang Software Engineer 

 Kaz Sato Staff Developer Advocate 

A guide to the new managed ingestion and SearchDocuments features in Agent Retrieval, for searching PDFs, Office files, and videos without writing an ingestion pipeline.

Before an agent can answer a question about your PDFs, someone has to build the pipeline: parse every file, split it into chunks, embed each chunk, write the chunks to a vector database, and then learn that database's schema to query it. For video it gets harder: transcode the files, cut them into clips, embed the frames, and keep track of which second of which video each clip came from.

 Before: every step of the pipeline is custom code you write and maintain, separately for documents and for videos. 

Most of that code has nothing to do with your application. Two features recently added to Agent Retrieval (formerly Vector Search 2.0), now in Public Preview, take that work off your hands. Managed ingestion builds the pipeline for you: point a data store at files in Cloud Storage, and the service parses, segments, and embeds them with Gemini Embedding 2. SearchDocuments, the second new feature, then searches the data store with one API call and returns the matching passages with their page numbers or timestamps. In our tests, 18 Alphabet investor PDFs went from a public Cloud Storage bucket to searchable, page cited results in about 9 minutes, and 19 minutes of video became searchable by both visuals and spoken audio in 0.3 to 0.5 seconds per query, with no parsing, chunking, transcription, or embedding code.

This guide covers how to create a data store, import documents and videos, and search them with filters, reranking, and audio-aware video search.

### What Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments Enable

 After: create separate data stores for documents (UNSTRUCTURED) and videos (VIDEO), point each at Cloud Storage, and search each with one SearchDocuments call that returns cited results. 

Pairing managed ingestion with SearchDocuments gives you several immediate benefits:

- No Ingestion Pipeline: Import PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, and TXT files, or MP4, MOV, WebM, MKV, and other video formats, straight from Cloud Storage. Parsing, segmentation, embedding, and the vector Collection and its schema are handled for you.
- Answers With Citations: Every result carries its source file URI and a page range for documents, or a start and end time for videos, so your agent can cite exactly where an answer came from.
- One Call to Search: SearchDocuments takes a data store and a text query. You don't pass a Collection name, a vector field, a task type, or output fields, and hybrid search (semantic + full-text) runs automatically for documents.
- Search What Was Said in Videos: Turn on audio embedding and a query matches the moment a speaker mentions a topic, even when the picture shows something else. No transcript or captions required.

...

### How It Works in Practice

1. Hybrid Retrieval: SearchDocuments runs a semantic search and a full-text search over the backing Collection and fuses the two result lists, so both paraphrased questions and exact terms match.
2. Segment-Level Results: Results are pages or chunks, not whole files. Several results can come from the same document, each with its own page range.
3. Optional Reranking: With reranking on, SearchDocuments retrieves more candidates than `top_k` and reorders them with the Ranking API, using the same `semantic-ranker-fast@latest` model as Agent Retrieval's `VertexRanker`.

...

### Requirements & Next Steps

- Regions: During Public Preview, only us-east4 or europe-west4
- API: Data store and SearchDocuments APIs at v1beta, called over REST (Python SDK support is planned)
- Permissions: Grant roles/vectorsearch.serviceAgent to the Agent Retrieval service agent so it can read your files

signals.title: Inkling 2 Mini Turns Repeated Computation Into a Local-Model Design Choice · Hugging Face Blog
signals.excerpt:
Inkling 2 Mini contains 24 physical decoder layers. The middle 12 are revisited three times, producing 48 logical layer visits: six initial layers, three passes through the 12-layer core, and six final layers. The repeated passes share weights, with learned messages carrying information between passes. Each visit routes a token to eight experts selected from 128.

This structure separates weight capacity from compute depth. Reusing weights can reduce how many distinct layer parameters must be stored, but every repeated visit still performs work. It also needs runtime state, including attention caches.

...

Checkpoint format influences storage and weight memory; active experts influence computation per token; context length influences cache memory; and logical depth influences latency.

...

## The variable-loop checkpoint exposes the tradeoff

Alongside the fixed three-pass model, the release includes a research checkpoint that can run the looped core one, two, or three times. Fewer passes are intended to make inference faster, with a possible reduction in output quality. The release authors say they have not evaluated that variant deeply, so it should be treated as an experimental control rather than a guaranteed performance dial.

...

## Local deployment still requires a memory budget

Support spans Transformers, llama.cpp-based tooling, MLX, and SGLang. The release provides four-bit and eight-bit GGUF variants for local runtimes, while MLX can use the original mixed-precision checkpoint. SGLang targets datacenter serving and can optionally use a DSpark draft model for speculative decoding. These options broaden access, but they are not interchangeable representations with identical behavior.

Before downloading weights, estimate four separate budgets:

1. Weight memory: quantization can reduce it, but runtime overhead and model metadata still count.
2. Context memory: a supported maximum is not the same as a practical operating length. Cache use grows with the active sequence and concurrency.
3. Compute time: 48 logical visits remain 48 visits even when some weights are shared.
4. Auxiliary memory: image processing, draft models, server buffers, and concurrent requests add to the total.

Start with a realistic context target rather than the advertised maximum. Measure first-token delay and generation rate at that length, then repeat with the concurrency the application actually needs.

signals.title: Mellum2.1 Instruct Is Out, Bringing Faster Answers for Coding Agents - The JetBrains Blog
signals.excerpt:
In October, we released Mellum2.1 Thinking, an open 12B mixture-of-experts model with 2.5B active parameters, trained to work as a coding agent. Today, we are releasing its sibling, Mellum2.1 Instruct. It is built on the same architecture and trained identically, but it gives straight answers without including its chain of thought.

What sets Mellum2.1 apart from Mellum2 is its post-training phase: large-scale reinforcement learning on repository-level tasks in real environments, built on NVIDIA NeMo open-source training libraries – NeMo RL and NeMo Megatron-Bridge for efficient large-scale distributed training.

As promised, this October we released the multi-token prediction (MTP) head for Mellum2.1 Thinking, making token generation up to 1.8x faster. Mellum2.1 Instruct is released together with its MTP head.

## Why an Instruct model, and when to use it

Reasoning models, such as Mellum2.1 Thinking, are a good fit for tasks that require a step-by-step approach, like finding the root cause of a failing test. But much of a coding agent’s work is simpler, like a small fix, a command to run, or a question about the code. In these cases, reasoning adds time and computing resources without adding quality.

This is especially true when the model runs locally – every extra thinking token adds to the time you’re waiting. After the Thinking release, we received many requests from the local-inference community for a more concise model for moderately hard tasks.

That is where Mellum2.1 Instruct fits in – either on its own or as the fast worker next to a stronger model. On agentic coding tasks, it generates about half as many tokens as the Thinking variant and performs almost as well on SWE-bench Verified. On hard algorithmic and math problems, such as those in LiveCodeBench and AIME, thinking is crucial, and so Mellum2.1 Thinking remains the better choice.

 

 

## Performance on benchmarks

We compared Mellum2.1 Instruct with its predecessor, Mellum2 Instruct, and two open models in the same class, Qwen3.5 9B and Gemma 4 E4B, both with thinking turned off.

The biggest gain is on the agentic benchmark SWE-bench Verified, where the score doubled compared with the previous Instruct release. The new training also improved code generation, where Mellum2.1 Instruct now leads the group, and multi-step tool use, where it is level with Qwen3.5 9B.

Qwen3.5 9B scores higher on SWE-bench Verified, but Mellum2.1 activates only 2.5B parameters per token. As a result, it generates tokens about 1.4x faster than Qwen3.5 9B for a single request and about 1.8x faster under load, as shown in our October post.

## How we trained it

Mellum2.1 Instruct went through the same two reinforcement learning stages as Thinking. First, it learned to solve standalone tasks in code, math, tool use, and instruction following. Then it learned to work as an agent in real repositories, using shell and file tools inside a sandbox and being rewarded only when the hidden tests passed.

We made two adjustments for Instruct. We tuned the length penalty for a model that answers without thinking, which keeps its answers concise and reduces the number of tokens without sacrificing quality. We also brought generation and training into closer agreement, which makes training more stable.

Both stages are built on NVIDIA NeMo open-source training libraries. NeMo RL, a post-training library, runs generation and training asynchronously, and NeMo Megatron-Bridge handles the weight updates across the large-scale distributed clusters of NVIDIA H200 and B300 GPUs. Together they let a single run collect about half a million agent trajectories from 10,000 concurrent sandboxes.

This release builds on open research, frameworks, and datasets. That is why Mellum2.1 is also open for others to build on.

...

Both variants of Mellum2.1 are available on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. Each one also comes in two additional versions:

- GGUF files for running the model on your own machine (Instruct, Thinking).
- A multi-token prediction (MTP) head that makes generation up to 1.8x faster (Instruct, Thinking).

signals.title: A ~45 MB control plane for 1,000+ GPU nodes — GPUWorks is now Apache 2.0 - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
On November 5 we open-sourced GPUWorks under Apache 2.0. It's a ~45 MB inference platform that turns the GPU servers a team already has into one shared cluster, with no Kubernetes underneath.

We built it because four questions kept coming back:

- A handful of GPU servers doesn't justify a full orchestration stack.
- "Heterogeneous support" usually means a compatibility table nobody reads. Teams want to know which card runs which model today.
- GPU partitioning helps small models. It does nothing for three large models competing for one 8-card group.
- Inference accounting rarely survives contact with reality, so nobody knows which card-hours go to which app.

## What it actually does 

Install in about a minute. One command completes the platform installation and deployment; additional GPU nodes are connected from the browser console. No pre-built Kubernetes, and offline import is supported for packages, weights and runtime images. 

```
bash <(curl -fsSL https://dl.gpuworks.ai/get.sh)

```

Serve with an OpenAI-compatible API. 1,000+ launch configurations covering roughly 400 models. A configuration bundles the image, inference engine, weight version and startup parameters into one deployment.

Share one GPU pool across large models. Priority, idle-yield and scheduled-rotation policies let multiple large models take turns on the same cards. L1 sleep keeps weights in host memory, so a sleeping model wakes in about 4 seconds instead of reloading from storage.

On an 8x H20 test, cold start from NFS took 16 to 17.5 minutes; wake-up took about 4 seconds.

Grow from one node to a thousand. In a real-machine test, one GPUWorks Server managed 1,003 GPU servers, brought up 500+ inference replicas in four minutes, and pushed 69,000 tokens per second, while the server process used 9 CPU cores and 1.6 GB of memory.

Mix vendors deliberately. NVIDIA, AMD, Huawei Ascend, T-Head PPU, Hygon DCU and others, across bare metal, VMs and cloud containers. The platform filters hardware by model compatibility instead of leaving it to a spreadsheet. RDMA and Ascend HCCS links are discovered and managed automatically.

See where compute goes. Token usage and cache hit rates by API key, model and deployment, alongside GPU occupancy and card-hours per million output tokens.

signals.title: Google & MongoDB launch AI agent integration
signals.excerpt:
Mon, 23rd Nov 2026 

 DAVID SHILOVSKY Interviews Editor 

Google and MongoDB have introduced a MongoDB integration for Google's Agent Development Kit, adding session storage, memory and retrieval features for AI agents.

The software connects MongoDB with Google's open-source ADK framework, which is used to build, debug and deploy AI agents. It is designed to let developers store agent sessions and longer-term memory in MongoDB, while using MongoDB Search to retrieve operational data.

Google's ADK is available in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java and Kotlin. The new integration centres on ADK 2.0, which Google describes as the orchestration layer for multi-agent systems, with MongoDB providing storage for sessions and memory.

According to the companies, the aim is to give developers a single data layer for application data, agent state and retrieval tasks. This is intended to reduce the need for separate databases or synchronisation pipelines when moving an AI agent from prototype to production.

Session storage

A key part of the release is the MongoDbSessionService class, which stores sessions, events, and application, user and session state in MongoDB. It includes optimistic concurrency control to help applications manage concurrent updates safely, along with configurable collections to fit existing data architectures.

The integration also includes a MongoDbMemoryService class for agents that need memory beyond a single session. It ingests session events into MongoDB collections and retrieves relevant memories through keyword matching.

MongoDB says memory ingestion is idempotent, helping to avoid duplication if an application adds the same session more than once. Developers can use the service to add a session to memory and search stored memory for relevant information tied to a user or application.

Search tools

The release also adds MongoDbToolset support for AI agents that need access to product catalogues, documents or other operational records already stored in MongoDB. This lets agents call search tools within ADK while the application retains control of the database connection, configuration and index settings.

According to the companies, the search component supports semantic and hybrid retrieval. In practice, this means developers can build agents for tasks such as product discovery, knowledge assistance, support workflows and specialised copilots using the same database layer.

Support covers MongoDB Atlas as well as self-managed MongoDB 8.0 and newer deployments for vector and hybrid search. Developers can connect through a connection string or use an existing PyMongo client, and can configure index names, embedding fields, result limits and candidate counts through MongoDbToolSettings.

Production focus

The integration reflects a broader shift in the AI software market as companies try to move agents from demonstrations into operational systems that can preserve user context across multiple interactions. In that environment, session persistence and memory have become central design questions alongside model choice.

Google says ADK supplies the framework and tool interface, while the MongoDB integration provides the persistence layer beneath it. The setup is intended to support agents that maintain conversation history independently of a single machine and carry a user's history across sessions.

The underlying ADK platform integrates with Gemini models, including Gemini 4 Argon for multi-step reasoning and Gemini 3.8 Flash for lower-latency execution. The companies say ADK 2.0 also provides standardised tool-calling interfaces, native telemetry and access controls.

The software can be installed through the Python package manager using the google-adk[mongodb] package, adding MongoDB support directly into ADK development environments.

signals.title: Improving AI efficiency with optimization | MIT Sloan
signals.excerpt:
## Finding the right balance between a model’s size and accuracy

Mazumder leads a team of researchers at the MIT Operations Research Center in exploring how large-scale mathematical optimization techniques — which find their use in supply chain, logistics, energy grid operations, and machine learning — can be used to balance model utility, data, computational workloads, hardware usage, and other parameters to extract high value from AI models while still being resource-efficient.

The reasoning behind the research is simple, he said. General-purpose AI models are good at many tasks but typically demand significant resources.

In contrast, it’s possible that high-performance models that are narrowly focused — on detecting defects on a factory floor or ranking products in search queries for a particular retailer, for example — might still be high-performing while relying on fewer resources.

A model running on a phone faces different resource limitations than one running on a factory sensor or in a data center, Mazumder said. Optimization helps determine the right balance between a model’s size, computational demands, and performance for each case.

## Optimization applied to model compression

Mazumder’s team develops large-scale optimization algorithms for AI model compression, the process of shrinking AI models so they use fewer resources. Say the mandate is to compress the model so it sacrifices 1% of accuracy compared with the original, uncompressed model. There will be disagreement as to what percentage of the model to compress to achieve that goal, he said.

Optimization helps teams decide what to remove and how much utility to retain within a given computing budget, Mazumder said, and provides everyone with a common language for weighing those trade-offs.

“The model optimization takes into account task-specific data, whether you care about industrial analytics or ranking a product,” as well as any compute-aware hardware constraints, he explained.

To that end, Mazumder and his team developed ADMM-Q, a procedure for quantizing LLMs, which he presented at the Conference on Language Modeling in October.

During his talk, Mazumder showed that an 8-billion-parameter AI model that was compressed with ADMM-Q answered a question noticeably faster than the uncompressed original. Compression can make serving a model one-and-a-half-times faster, he said, and has implications for both energy and GPU savings.

What sets ADMM-Q apart, he said, is accuracy: The research team found that models compressed with ADMM-Q retained more of the original model’s performance than those compressed with standard methods, especially when the model was made much smaller.

Ultimately, Mazumder said, his goal is to see whether it’s possible to design high-performing AI models while ensuring that they are resource-efficient. If it is, more-capable models could run directly on phones and laptops rather than in the cloud, which would help democratize AI access.

signals.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
signals.excerpt:
Over the past three months, we have aggressively scaled both loop depth and model size in parallel. The first surprise came from the Loop Transformer architecture itself. By executing a shared block of layers across multiple iterations, the model can reason more deeply without adding parameters, effectively matching the performance of much larger models.

- GLM-5.4 is our first flagship model built on the Loop Transformer architecture, reaching intelligence levels comparable to 2T-3T parameter models.
- GLM-5.4 marks the start of Generalized Coding, where code becomes the foundation for solving a much wider range of tasks and unlocking new capabilities.

The model still has some limitations. Most notably, it tends to get caught in overly long "marathon thinking" loops, though this prolonged reflection and self-correction does consistently improve accuracy beyond its parameter count.

...

In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count.

The idea is not new. ... Instead of pre-training from scratch, we adapted an already pre-trained base model into a Loop Transformer through continued training. This lets us raise the intelligence ceiling with a relatively small compute overhead.

## Architectural Modifications at 750B Scale

GLM-5.4 loops 28 layers of the GLM-5 base model for two iterations. To balance performance gains with deployment costs at the 750B scale, we made three changes after extensive experimentation:

#### Gated Progressive Updates

When converting middle layers of an existing model into a multi-pass loop, directly overwriting hidden states causes activation norms to blow up across iterations. Downstream layers then receive representations outside their expected scale and distribution.

GLM-5.4 adds independent per-token gates for each iteration to proportionally write candidate updates back into the residual stream. After training, these gates develop a clear division of labor. The first pass builds global context and writes conservatively with small gate values to keep scales stable. The second pass reuses this state to refine the output, opening the gates to write full updates. The gates also adjust step size dynamically based on token difficulty: on harder tokens, the first pass writes more aggressively so complex predictions benefit more from iterative refinement.

#### Hybrid KV Cache (Global Sharing + Independent Sliding Window)

A naive implementation keeps a full KV cache for every loop iteration, multiplying memory usage with the loop count. Instead, we build on cross-loop KV sharing by supplementing it with a local sliding window for the new pass: the second loop reuses the sparse KV selected in the first pass, while retaining its own newly generated KV within the sliding window. These two KV streams can overlap at the same positions, allowing the model to attend to both the first-pass context representations and the updated local representations from the second pass.

As a result, an extra loop only costs one sliding window of KV cache rather than a full context cache. At 1M context lengths, this keeps GLM-5.4’s deployment cost increase over GLM-5.3 well under control.

#### Sparse Attention Index Reuse

GLM-5.4’s base model uses sparse attention. The second loop directly reuses the attention indices generated by the first loop's indexer, adding zero indexing overhead. Our experiments show this performs nearly identically to recomputing indices on every pass.

## Scaling Correctness & Controlled Iso-Parameter Ablations

Looping is also a strict test of Scaling Correctness: any architectural change must still work at scale. Before committing our flagship model to it, we validated the Loop architecture progressively across 1B, 4B, 30B, and 750B base models.

On a 30B model with the exact same architecture as our 750B base, we ran a controlled iso-parameter comparison. With identical parameter counts and only ~10% more total training compute, the looped version showed clear gains:

(Evaluated on the 30B model after 200K long-context SFT, with thinking mode enabled.)

Two findings stand out:

- Longer reasoning chains benefit more. The largest gains show up in math, scientific reasoning, and long-context tasks, which are core to Generalized Coding.
- Fewer tokens spent on thinking. Across most benchmarks like GPQA-Diamond and MMLU-Pro, average output length drops by 10–14%, mostly from shorter chains of thought. In effect, part of the reasoning shifts from explicit output tokens into the implicit depth of the loop.

## Inference Efficiency

GLM-5.4 reaches up to 200 tokens/s during off-peak hours and maintains 70–80 tokens/s at peak load. Achieving this throughput with a multi-pass Loop architecture required close co-design between the model and our inference infrastructure. Alongside the memory and retrieval savings from our KV cache and sparse index designs, we fused core kernels at the systems level to cut down intermediate memory reads and writes, eliminating the fragmented overhead amplified by looping.

signals.title: Amazon Releases Open-weight Strands Decider V2 Models - Dataconomy
signals.excerpt:
Amazon has released five open-weight Strands Decider v2 models, built on Gemma 4, with a new architecture intended to improve choices that depend on a single detail in a long input.

The Apache 2.0-licensed model family ranges up to 31 billion parameters. It lets developers provide up to 255 options for each multiple-choice question and returns a probability for every option.

AWS said its largest v2 model scored 71.5 on the public Decision Index 0.3 benchmark, compared with 48.8 for the largest Strands Decider v1 model. The comparison used the 31B v2 model and the 26B-A4B v1 model, rather than models of equivalent size.

On DecisionPivot, a StartLux benchmark based on pairs that differ by one decisive detail, AWS said the largest v2 model scored 84.3, versus 23.2 for the v1 model.

Fabio Nonato de Paula, a principal applied scientist at AWS, said feedback on Strands Decider v1 showed that users wanted stronger performance on difficult cases in which one detail changes the outcome. AWS released v1 on October 1.

“With v2, you can ask many questions about one situation and pay to read that situation only once, so we basically changed how the model reads a scenario,” Nonato de Paula said.

AWS said v2 reads a situation in both directions and creates a shared representation that each question uses to score its options. V1 could also reuse shared input across questions, but v2 changes how the input is read and represented. AWS said developers can use a new option set without retraining the model.

...

AWS said teams can download, fine-tune and run Strands models on their own infrastructure. Gemma 4 is also licensed under Apache 2.0, comes in sizes AWS requires, accepts images and text at every size, and has a smallest version that can run without a GPU.

signals.excerpt:

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MemTensor today released and open-sourced MemT-1.0-Pro, a memory-native model jointly developed with NVIDIA.

Built on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra and trained using NVIDIA's Megatron-Core and Megatron Bridge distributed training infrastructure, MemT-1.0-Pro extends MemTensor's memory-native approach to 554 billion total parameters, with 59 billion active parameters. Following Nano and Flash, the release advances this exploration on a new backbone and at a larger model scale.

 

Architecture of MemT 1.0: integrating dynamic local memory and trainable hyper-memory into model computation.

MemT-1.0-Pro integrates memory into model computation, making the storage, updating and retrieval of historical information capabilities that can be learned through training.

The collaboration with NVIDIA included model adaptation, operator optimization, training-method discussions and experimental review.

Extending MemTensor's Memory-Native Approach to Nemotron

MemT-1.0-Pro uses NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-BF16 as its backbone. Its architecture combines dynamic local memory, which stores information acquired during interaction, with trainable hyper-memory components that learn how to write and read that information.

During online interaction, the backbone and trained memory-processing weights remain fixed. The model accesses historical information through dynamic memory states, without requiring the original historical text to remain in the query context. After each completed interaction, a storage procedure updates those states using a stabilized token-level mechanism based on Gated DeltaNet-2.

Continued pre-training establishes language modeling capabilities that use native memory. Post-training then uses distillation from a full-context teacher to improve memory-based responses.

Measurable Progress in Long-History Memory

In the technical report, MemT-1.0-Pro scores 41.80 on BEAM-1M, compared with 37.04 for MemT-1.0-Flash, an improvement of 4.76 points. On MemoryAgentBench, its score rises to 23.87 from 17.36, a gain of 6.51 points.

BEAM-1M evaluates ten long-history memory abilities, including information extraction, contradiction resolution, updating, preference following and temporal reasoning. MemoryAgentBench evaluates retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding and selective forgetting.

Pro also achieves an average score of 53.08 across 11 memory benchmarks, the highest among the parametric-memory methods evaluated in the report.

These results demonstrate progress within the MemT family, although Flash and Pro use different backbones and configurations, and improvements vary across benchmarks. Strong textual-memory systems remain ahead on some evaluations.

...

These needs motivate MemTensor's exploration of native memory for persistent agent workflows. Further application testing will be needed to establish how the benchmark gains translate into end-to-end task performance.

Fixed-size memory introduces trade-offs between preserving earlier details and incorporating new information. Improving memory fidelity, selective retention and query-dependent readout remains central to further research.

Developers and researchers are welcome to explore MemT-1.0-Pro on Hugging Face.

signals.title: TensorRT-LLM V1.3.0 Brings NVFP4 To Hopper And Ada, Drops Legacy Backend | Smart Chunks
signals.excerpt:
November 22, 2026

...

## TL;DR

- NVIDIA’s TensorRT-LLM v1.3.0 adds MXFP8, an 8-bit number format, for standard layers and mixture-of-experts layers.
- A new 4-bit, weight-only NVFP4 path built on Marlin means NVFP4 checkpoints now run on Hopper and Ada Lovelace GPUs.
- NVFP4 quantization is now tunable, and PyTorch is the only backend left.
- The practical upshot: more NVIDIA GPUs can serve newer compressed models.

## Two new low-precision paths and one big deletion

Quantization means storing a model’s numbers with fewer bits. Fewer bits means a smaller memory footprint. NVIDIA’s TensorRT-LLM v1.3.0 release adds two new ways to do that.

The first is MXFP8, written as W8A8. That label means the weights (the numbers the model learned) and the activations (the values it computes while running) both use 8 bits. Support covers linear layers, the basic matrix-math blocks, and MoE layers. MoE is short for mixture of experts: a model split into specialist sub-networks, where only a few work on each token.

The release notes name MiniMax-M3 as one supported MXFP8 checkpoint. A checkpoint is simply a saved set of model weights. The exact line reads: “Added MXFP8 (W8A8) linear and MoE support, including MXFP8 checkpoints such as MiniMax-M3.”

The second path is the one I’d watch. NVIDIA “added W4A16 NVFP4 weight-only quantization through Marlin, so NVFP4 checkpoints run on Hopper and Ada Lovelace.” Translation: weights are stored in 4 bits while activations stay at 16. Marlin is a set of GPU kernels, the small programs that do the actual math. Hopper and Ada Lovelace are two NVIDIA GPU generations.

The release also adds tunable NVFP4 quantization. It supports both legacy and ModelOpt 1.x quantization config formats. The notes don’t spell out what “tunable” lets you adjust.

...

And that’s the trade. You get a smaller footprint without asking every layer to run at 4 bits. The release notes don’t say how much speed or memory you actually gain, so I won’t guess.

...

## The quieter change: PyTorch is now the only backend

TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA’s open-source library for optimizing and serving large language models on its GPUs. A backend is the engine underneath that actually executes the model. Version 1.3.0 removes the legacy TensorRT backend, which leaves PyTorch as the sole backend.

That’s a major architectural change. It also means fewer code paths to maintain and test. For NVIDIA, new quantization formats now have one place to land.

For users, the picture is less tidy. Anyone whose setup still leans on the old backend will need to check their workflow before upgrading. The support for legacy and ModelOpt 1.x config formats looks like a bridge for existing quantization setups. The notes don’t say how smooth that bridge is.
